artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a field (for instance $\mathbb{R}$, or a finite field). Given a finite collection $\mathcal{L}$ of lines in $\mathbb{F}^3$, call a point $p \in \mathbb{F}^3$ a joint of $\mathcal{L}$ if there exist three lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3 \in \mathcal{L}$ all passing through $p$ whose direction vectors are linearly independent (i.e., the three lines are not coplanar).

For a positive integer $n$, define
$$J_{\mathbb{F}}(n) = \max\{\,|\text{Joints}(\mathcal{L})| : \mathcal{L} \text{ is a set of } n \text{ lines in } \mathbb{F}^3\,\}.$$

Determine the asymptotic behavior of $J_{\mathbb{F}}(n)$ as $n \to \infty$. In particular, it is known that there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ and configurations of $n$ lines with at least $c\, n^{3/2}$ joints, and the trivial upper bound is $O(n^2)$. Find the correct order of magnitude of $J_{\mathbb{R}}(n)$, and the analogous quantity when $\mathbb{R}$ is replaced by a finite field.
artifact.status_search_result: The joints problem was solved by Guth and Katz, who proved that n lines in R^3 determine at most O(n^{3/2}) joints, matching the lower bound. The polynomial-method proof was subsequently extended to arbitrary fields (e.g., by Quilodrán, Kaplan–Sharir–Shustin, and others), giving the same n^{3/2} bound over any field including finite fields. Sharp constants have been further refined (e.g., by Yu and Zhao).

status_evidence.title: Joints of varieties (Yufei Zhao)
status_evidence.snippet: Guth and Katz proved that N lines in R^3 have O(N^{3/2}) joints; Yu and Zhao sharpened the constant.
status_evidence.claim: The joints problem in R^3 is solved with the tight bound Θ(n^{3/2}).

status_evidence.title: On Lines, Joints, and Incidences in Three Dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: Extends the joints bound and gives O(n^{3/2}) for joints of n lines in three dimensions.
status_evidence.claim: The n^{3/2} upper bound holds for joints in 3 dimensions, including extensions to other fields.

status_evidence.title: The joints problem in R^n (Quilodrán)
status_evidence.snippet: Polynomial-method proof of the joints bound extending to higher dimensions and general fields.
status_evidence.claim: The polynomial-method proof works over general fields, including finite fields.
